Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the case lacks critical information that directly determines surgical feasibility, namely a quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and detailed anatomic relationship of the remaining lesions to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures. Until these data are obtained, a definitive decision on upfront resection cannot be made; the patient may become resectable after confirming adequate FLR or after adjunctive measures such as portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a staged approach.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy with the current FOLFOXIRI regimen (or add a biologic agent if molecular profile warrants) to maximise tumour shrinkage; aim for a total of 6–8 cycles unless toxicity limits treatment.  
• Serial monitoring of CEA and repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary contrast) after each 2‑cycle block to document response and to identify lesions that have become amenable to resection or ablation.  
• At the time of maximal radiologic response, perform a comprehensive restaging work‑up:  
   – Volumetric liver CT/MRI to calculate FLR (target ≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   – High‑resolution imaging of the hepatic hilum and major veins to define proximity of residual lesions to portal/hepatic veins and biliary confluence.  
   – Chest CT and pelvic MRI (or endorectal ultrasound) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Assessment of performance status, liver function tests, and chemotherapy‑related liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
• Multidisciplinary decision based on the above data:  
   – If FLR is adequate and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection. For bilobar disease, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if rapid hypertrophy is needed.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolisation (or ligation) to induce hypertrophy, re‑image after 2–4 weeks, and then proceed to resection.  
   – For lesions abutting major vessels where a safe margin cannot be obtained, plan intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided ablation (RFA or microwave) combined with limited resection.  
• Management of the primary rectal tumour:  
   – If the rectal lesion is asymptomatic and down‑staged, a liver‑first approach is preferred; after hepatic surgery, deliver standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (long‑course 5‑FU‑based) followed by low anterior resection.  
   – If the rectal tumour is symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction) or requires urgent treatment, perform resection of the primary first, then resume systemic therapy and reassess hepatic resectability.  
• Post‑operative plan: adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of planned cycles) and consider maintenance biologic therapy based on molecular profile; enrol in surveillance programme with 3‑monthly CEA and 6‑monthly imaging for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver).  
• Exact number, maximal diameter, and segmental distribution of the residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
• Relationship of each lesion to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes).  
• Current status of the primary rectal tumour (local stage, symptoms, need for radiotherapy).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
• Evidence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
• Molecular profile of the tumour (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to guide targeted therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

The recommendations include the same case-specific clinical details and patient-related factors, such as molecular profile implications, lesion-specific surgical considerations, and patient-level factors relevant to treatment sequencing. Additionally, they identify the same essential missing clinical information, including quantitative future liver remnant volume, exact number and distribution of residual liver lesions, and presence or absence of extra-hepatic metastases.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the current imaging shows three residual liver lesions <2 cm after chemotherapy, which suggests technical feasibility, but definitive classification requires (a) a quantitative assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve, and (b) confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum, distant nodes). Without these decisive pieces of information we cannot label the case as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy to complete an optimal pre‑operative regimen (e.g., 6–8 cycles total). Because the tumour is RAS wild‑type, add an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) to the doublet if not already used, to maximise tumour kill and provide a “proof of time” for tumour biology.  
• Restage after the planned total chemotherapy course:  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to re‑measure each lesion and map segmental location.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight ratio), plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
• If restaging confirms ≤3 lesions, no extra‑hepatic disease, and adequate FLR, schedule curative‑intent liver surgery:  
   – Perform intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion number and location.  
   – Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 mm microscopic margin; consider parenchymal‑sparing segmental or subsegmental resections.  
   – For lesions abutting major vessels where safe resection would sacrifice too much parenchyma, use adjunctive thermal ablation (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy to achieve complete local control.  
• Address the primary rectal tumour after hepatic clearance (or simultaneously if anatomy and patient condition allow):  
   – If the rectal tumour is still present, give long‑course chemoradiotherapy followed by low anterior resection or abdominoperineal excision, depending on sphincter involvement.  
   – If the primary has already been resected, ensure clear margins and adequate lymphadenectomy.  
• Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy for 3–6 months, preferably the same regimen that achieved response, to eradicate microscopic disease.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; cross‑sectional imaging (MRI or CT) every 6 months for at least 3 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Precise segmental location of the three residual liver lesions and their relationship to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or functional liver reserve: indocyanine‑green clearance, liver function tests).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET, peritoneal assessment).  
• Status of the primary rectal tumour (still in situ, symptomatic, prior radiotherapy, need for resection).  
• Patient performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The case contains a decisive missing piece of information: the functional liver reserve (future liver remnant volume) and the anatomic distribution of the seven remaining metastases (unilobar vs bilobar, proximity to major vessels). Without these data a safe R0 resection cannot be confirmed, and the single progressing 5‑cm lesion in segment VII may require down‑staging before surgery. Therefore the patient cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” based on current oncologic or anatomic contraindications.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Confirm primary‑tumor status – if the left‑sided colon primary has not yet been resected, plan either (a) simultaneous colon‑liver resection (if the liver operation will be limited) or (b) staged resection with the liver first (“reverse” approach) because a major hepatectomy is likely required.  
2. Systemic therapy continuation – KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents; continue an oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab) or intensify to FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab if the patient is fit (ECOG 0‑1, adequate marrow, renal and hepatic function).  
3. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months (≈ 6–8 weeks of chemotherapy): repeat triphasic CT/MRI with volumetric analysis.  
   - If all lesions are now ≤ 5 cm, no vascular encasement, and the projected FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % after chemotherapy), proceed to surgical planning.  
   - If the segment VII lesion remains progressive, consider local ablative control (RFA or stereotactic body radiotherapy) to achieve down‑staging.  
4. Pre‑operative liver optimisation – if volumetry shows FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (resection of lesions in one lobe, PVE, then completion hepatectomy).  
5. Surgical plan – aim for an R0 resection of all viable disease:  
   - Major hepatectomy (right or extended right) to include the segment VII lesion, combined with parenchymal‑sparing resections (non‑anatomical wedge or segmentectomy) for the remaining stable lesions, preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
   - If any lesion is unresectable due to vascular proximity, treat it with intra‑operative ablation (RFA/ microwave) to achieve negative margins.  
6. Post‑operative management – resume the same systemic regimen (or an adapted one if toxicity occurred) for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy, unless contraindicated.  
7. Surveillance – CT/MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, with CEA monitoring.

Step 3 – Missing data (essential for a definitive recommendation)  
- Performance status (ECOG/WHO) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and Child‑Pugh score.  
- Detailed imaging of the liver: exact number, size, and segmental location of each of the six stable lesions; relationship to major hepatic veins, portal/hepatic arteries, and biliary structures.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) before and after chemotherapy.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, or pending resection).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Current chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles already delivered, and response criteria (RECIST) for each lesion.  
- Laboratory tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9) trends.  

These data are required to finalize resectability, choose the optimal systemic regimen, and decide on the need for portal vein embolisation or staged hepatectomy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Recommendation 1 considers the patient as potentially resectable with a plan for systemic therapy and potential surgical intervention, while Recommendation 2 deems the patient unresectable at this stage and focuses on adapting systemic therapy and considering selective local strategies. The missing data required for a definitive recommendation also show discrepancies between the two, highlighting a lack of concordance across all evaluated criteria.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient shows a radiological complete response after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but current evidence indicates that microscopic residual disease may persist in sites of previously documented metastases. Definitive cure therefore still requires surgical clearance of the original hepatic disease (or at least a confirmatory intra‑operative assessment). Because the decision hinges on a prerequisite surgical action – namely exploration with intra‑operative ultrasound and resection (or ablative treatment) of the prior lesion sites – the case fits the “Potentially resectable” definition. No absolute anatomic or functional contraindication is reported, but essential data needed to confirm technical feasibility are missing.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Confirm disease status before any operation  
   - Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) to reassess for any occult lesions.  
   - Perform a PET‑CT to evaluate for residual extra‑hepatic disease (especially the lungs).  

2. Assess primary rectal tumor  
   - Review baseline rectal staging (MRI pelvis) and current status (symptoms, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
   - If the primary remains unresected, plan standard rectal cancer protocol (short‑course radiotherapy or long‑course chemoradiation) followed by curative‑intent low anterior resection (or abdominoperineal resection if required).  

3. Surgical plan for the liver  
   - Schedule a liver‑focused operation with a hepatobiliary surgeon experienced in parenchymal‑sparing techniques.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the original metastatic sites; even if no mass is visible, mark the segmental locations based on pre‑treatment imaging.  
   - Perform limited anatomical resections (segmentectomy/sectionectomy) or non‑anatomical wedge resections of those zones, aiming for R0 margins.  
   - If the future liver remnant (FLR) is estimated <30 % of total liver volume, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive resection.  
   - In cases where resection would be technically demanding, adjunctive ablative modalities (RFA, microwave ablation, or SBRT) may be employed to achieve complete clearance.  

4. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - After hepatic surgery (and primary resection if applicable), give adjuvant chemotherapy – preferably 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) without biologic agents, as peri‑operative biologics have not shown survival benefit in the resectable setting.  
   - If the primary tumor was not previously irradiated, incorporate the appropriate radiotherapy schedule before or after surgery according to standard rectal cancer guidelines.  

5. Follow‑up  
   - Serial CEA measurements every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Imaging surveillance with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

- Exact number, maximal diameter, and segmental distribution of the original liver metastases.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets, liver enzymes).  
- Presence, size, and number of any extra‑hepatic lesions (e.g., lung nodules) and their response to chemotherapy.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR status) to guide any targeted adjuvant considerations.  
- Current status of the rectal primary (clinical T/N stage, response to any prior radiotherapy, symptom burden).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  

These data are essential to finalize the operative plan, confirm that an adequate FLR will remain, and ensure that no residual extra‑hepatic disease precludes a curative approach.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The solitary 3.9 cm metastasis in segment VII can be removed with an anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge while preserving at least two contiguous segments (e.g., II‑III, VI‑VIII) and a future liver remnant well above the 30 % threshold. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified, and the lesion is anatomically approachable. KRAS mutation influences prognosis but does not preclude curative surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin), indocyanine‑green clearance or LiMAx, and volumetric CT/MRI to confirm FLR > 30 % (or >0.5 % body weight).  
   – Review performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and CEA level.  
   – Confirm that the primary colorectal tumor has already been resected with clear margins.  

• Surgical plan  
   – Perform a formal segment VII resection (anatomic segmentectomy) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm acceptable in modern series).  
   – Approach can be laparoscopic or open depending on surgeon expertise and intra‑operative ultrasound findings.  
   – Preserve inflow/outflow and biliary drainage of the remaining segments; no need for portal vein embolisation or two‑stage hepatectomy given the limited volume loss.  

• Post‑operative oncologic management  
   – Start adjuvant systemic chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   – Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective; consider adding bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) if tolerated.  
   – Plan for 3–6 months of adjuvant therapy, with surveillance imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first two years.  

• Alternative / adjunctive options (if liver function is borderline or patient is frail)  
   – Percutaneous radiofrequency ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy of segment VII lesion as a bridge or definitive treatment.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) and functional reserve assessment (ICG‑R15, LiMAx).  
• Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and detailed comorbidity profile (Charlson index).  
• Serum CEA level and any other tumour markers.  
• Confirmation that the primary colorectal tumour has been resected with negative margins and its pathological stage.  
• Baseline hepatic laboratory values (bilirubin, transaminases, INR, albumin).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and confirm preservation of portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the KRAS mutation and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to address potential micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing)
• Proceed with an ultrasound-guided wedge/segmental resection of segment VII aiming for R0 margins while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.

Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six metastases 2–4 cm each are technically resectable only if a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % can be preserved; the current CT does not provide volumetric data to confirm this.  
- The disease is synchronous, T4 N2, with very high CEA (320 ng/mL) and circulating tumor cells, indicating aggressive biology that traditionally prompts “proof of time” with neoadjuvant chemotherapy before committing to surgery.  
- Therefore a prerequisite systemic therapy (and/or volumetric liver assessment) is required before an R0 liver resection can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start a 3‑month intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status and high‑risk primary.  
   - Monitor CEA and circulating tumor cells after each cycle; repeat high‑resolution liver MRI or contrast‑enhanced CT at 8–12 weeks to assess tumor response and to perform volumetric FLR calculation.  

2. Re‑assessment of resectability  
   - If all lesions shrink or remain stable and FLR ≥30 % (or can be increased to that threshold), proceed to surgical planning.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  

3. Surgical sequence  
   - Primary colon tumor: perform oncologic left‑sided colectomy with en‑bloc resection of the T4 lesion (primary first) followed by recovery, unless the patient’s condition permits a simultaneous liver‑first approach.  
   - Liver metastases:  
     • If a single‑stage hepatectomy can achieve R0 resection with ≥2 contiguous segments preserved, perform it after primary resection.  
     • If bilobar disease precludes a single‑stage resection, adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy: first stage resect left‑lateral lesions (or those in segments 2‑4) and place PVE; after hypertrophy (≈4–6 weeks), complete right‑hemihepatectomy or extended resection to clear remaining lesions.  
     • For lesions in difficult locations, supplement resection with intra‑operative thermal ablation (RFA/SBRT) to achieve complete eradication.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic therapy for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, tailoring biologic agents to RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   - Serial CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, to detect recurrence early.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Performance status / ECOG score and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Precise segmental distribution of the six liver lesions and volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., chest CT, PET‑CT).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and indocyanine‑green clearance if available.  
- BRAF mutation status (although RAS is wild‑type, BRAF could further influence prognosis).  
- Details on vascular involvement of the primary tumor (e.g., involvement of mesenteric vessels) that may affect timing of colon resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases (2–4 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Despite the bilobar distribution, the number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The detection of circulating tumor cells reflects increased systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Mandatory peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all six lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
E. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
F. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.
